steps.text:
Reviewing a loss is the one study habit that keeps pointing your other study at the right thing. A drill trains one skill; a review tells you which skill the last game actually needed.

Your rate of leaving material hanging has been flat for two years of blitz, against weaker and stronger opponents alike. More games alone haven't moved it. A few minutes after a loss turns the game into one line: where it turned, what kind of mistake, and the question that would have caught it.

Keep it small or it won't last. Losses only. Three to five minutes. Not every game: one or two a day is plenty, and skip it when you're annoyed. It must not become another data project.

These cards teach the routine on your 30 most recent losses (2026-11-22 to 2026-11-25). Do a few at a time. After that, do the same thing on Lichess after your own games.

1. Gut call. Before looking at anything: why do you think you lost? One phrase. This is the part that trains your judgment, because you find out later whether you were right.

2. Step through with the engine off. No evaluation bar, no arrows. Just the moves and the clocks.

3. Find the turning point. The move of yours after which the game was never level again. Not the last blunder before resigning; the first moment it went from playable to lost. Then name it: what kind of mistake was it (next card)?

4. Turn the engine on and check. Did you find the same move? What was better? If the engine's move makes no sense to you even after a minute, save the position. That's a gap in understanding, and it's worth asking about.

5. Write one line. Move number, kind of mistake, clock, and the question that would have caught it. Example: Move 21, they could win material, 2:00 on the clock. Next time ask: after my move, what can they take?

Every turning point in these cards gets one of four names, plus a fifth for games the board didn't decide. Each name comes with the question that would have caught it.

They could win material. Your move let them take something, at once or after a short forcing line. Question: after my move, what can they take?

They had a mating attack. Your move let them in at your king. Question: after my move, what checks do they have?

I missed a win of my own. You had a forced mate or a material win and played something else. Question: before I move, what can I take, and what checks do I have?

Nothing was lost yet: my position just got worse. No material changes hands, but the engine's line leaves you clearly worse. Usually a quiet move without a plan. Question: what is my plan, and what does this move give them?

No move lost it. You lost on time with a good position, or resigned one. The review then is about the clock, not the moves.

How the cards decide the name: the engine's best line for each side over the next few moves, with pawn 1, piece 3, rook 5, queen 9. Losing 2 points or more counts as losing material.

In 20 of the 28 games where one move decided it, that move let your opponent do something forcing: win material (14 games) or start a mating attack (6). Look 1, “after my move, what can they take or check?”, would have been the question in most of these games.

The rest: 6 where your position just got worse with no material lost, and 2 where you missed a win of your own. In 1 game you lost on time from a good position, and in 1 you resigned a level one.

It wasn't the clock. At the turning point you had a median of 2:02 left (only 0 of 28 had under half a minute), and you spent a median of 7.5s on the deciding move, against 4s on a typical move from move 10 on. You took a bit longer and still missed it, which is the same picture as your two-year data: the time is there, the check isn't.

The turning point came around move 22, in the middlegame (range 11 to 43). In 14 of the 28 you had been winning earlier (70% chances or better) and let it go.

So what: expect the review to keep naming the same kind of mistake. That's useful, not boring: a tally of your one-line notes over a few weeks tells you whether the two looks are starting to stick.

How this was measured: Stockfish 16 at depth 16 on every position of the 30 games; deeper (depth 20) on each deciding move. Winning chances use Lichess's scale. The turning point is the first of your moves, once you had dropped below 40% for good, that cost at least 15 points of winning chances. Thirty games is a small sample: read the counts as rough shares, not exact rates.

After a loss on Lichess, open the game's analysis board and keep the computer evaluation switched off for steps 1 to 3. Step through with the arrows.

Step 4: switch the engine on, or request a computer analysis, and jump to the move you picked. The evaluation graph is a fast way to see whether the real turning point was earlier.

Step 5: one line in a note on your phone. Once a week, count the kinds. If one kind dominates, that's what your next ten-minute windows should go to.

If an engine move makes no sense after a minute, add the position to a Lichess study chapter. Those are worth bringing to a chat, or to a video on that idea.

Short on time? Steps 1, 3 and 5 alone are worth doing: the gut call, the turning point, the one line.
